case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party may seek relief under Rule 60(b)(4) from a default judgment void for lack of personal jurisdiction at any time, or whether Rule 60(c)(1) requires the motion to be filed within a "reasonable time."
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (relief from a judgment that "is void") and 60(c)(1) (any Rule 60(b) motion "must be made within a reasonable time"), with background Due Process Clause principles governing personal jurisdiction and notice.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Coney Island argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio (a legal nullity), so there can be no deadline—reasonable or otherwise—for a Rule 60(b)(4) motion challenging it. In its view, applying Rule 60(c)(1)’s "reasonable time" limitation to void-judgment motions improperly converts a jurisdictional defect into a waivable, time-barred issue, conflicting with the settled principle that void judgments can be attacked whenever the defect is raised. Petitioner also suggests that due process concerns should override equitable defenses like laches where personal jurisdiction was absent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Trustee argues that the text is straightforward: Rule 60(c)(1) says any motion "under Rule 60(b)"—including 60(b)(4)—must be made within a reasonable time, and the Sixth Circuit correctly enforced that requirement. Respondent emphasizes finality and reliance interests, particularly in bankruptcy where delayed attacks can disrupt or unwind a nearly administered estate, and notes potential prejudice because timely notice of a service/jurisdiction defect would have allowed corrective service earlier. Respondent also points to this Court’s recent statement that "[a]ll" Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (statement that "[a]ll" Rule 60(b) motions must be filed "within a reasonable time")
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa (discussion of Rule 60(b)(4) and voidness; cited for the proposition that void judgments may be attacked and for reliance on treatises/circuit authority)
Klapprott v. United States (early Rule 60 case; discussed as assuming no definite time limit for 60(b)(4) and reaching merits of voidness)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co. (inherent power to manage dockets; cited in the lower-court materials)
World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litigation (2d Cir. 2013) (inherent power/docket management; cited in the lower-court materials)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp. (2d Cir. 1970) (discretion/comity regarding which court should address a motion to vacate a registered judgment)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd. (2d Cir. 1993) (comity/discretion principles)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc. (1st Cir. 1990) (cited in connection with Espinosa and void-judgment timing discussion)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain persuaded that Rule 60(c)(1)’s directive that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be filed “within a reasonable time” naturally includes Rule 60(b)(4), with no textual basis for a categorical timeless exception. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces that reading and supports a narrow, rules-based disposition. The petitioner’s strongest point—that a void judgment is a nullity that may be attacked at any time—runs into Espinosa’s admonition (emphasized by Justice Kagan) that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a “license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” and our voidness doctrine is itself tightly confined. A minimalist holding applying (c)(1) to (b)(4), while leaving “reasonable time” to the lower courts’ fact-bound assessment, best protects finality and institutional legitimacy without foreclosing relief for genuinely jurisdictionally void judgments promptly challenged.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—the common-law maxim that a void judgment is a nullity attackable “at any time”—cannot overcome the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which says any motion “under Rule 60(b)” (including (b)(4)) “must be made within a reasonable time,” with no carveout. Justice Alito’s emphasis on finality and the danger of rewriting the Rule is consistent with a textualist approach: importing a categorical timeless exception would add words the Rule’s drafters did not include. Justice Kagan’s point about Klapprott matters because it confirms only that the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3) doesn’t apply to (b)(4), leaving (c)(1)’s freestanding reasonable-time requirement intact. Espinosa further supports enforcing diligence requirements, rejecting the idea that (b)(4) is a license to sleep on rights, so petitioner’s categorical position fails on the text and our precedents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the common-law maxim that a void judgment is a nullity challengeable “at any time,” but that principle cannot displace the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b),” including (b)(4). Chief Justice Roberts’s minimalist framing is right: we can enforce the reasonable-time requirement as written while leaving lower courts latitude to assess reasonableness case by case, including notice, prejudice, and reliance interests—especially salient in bankruptcy. Justice Kagan’s reminder that Espinosa rejects using Rule 60(b)(4) as a “license to sleep on rights,” and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Kemp’s statement that “all” 60(b) motions are subject to (c)(1), further undercut any categorical timeless carve-out. Klapprott, as multiple colleagues note, at most rejects the one-year bar for (b)(1)–(3), and does not erase (c)(1)’s independent reasonable-time command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—that a void judgment is a nullity attackable “at any time”—cannot overcome the Rules’ enacted timing directive: Rule 60(c)(1) applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b),” and nothing in the text carves out (b)(4). Justice Kagan’s reading of Klapprott is especially persuasive to me: it rejects importing the one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3) into (b)(4), but it does not displace the separate “reasonable time” requirement, so petitioner’s categorical timelessness argument lacks a textual anchor. Espinosa’s warning (highlighted by the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan) that 60(b)(4) is not “a license for litigants to sleep on their rights” fits a pragmatic, fairness-oriented approach because it protects vulnerable third parties and bankruptcy reliance interests from strategic delay while still allowing prompt relief for genuine jurisdictional or due-process failures. Kemp’s statement, emphasized by Justice Barrett, that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to (c)(1) further confirms that diligence can be required without watering down the narrow voidness doctrine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack “at any time”—has force at common law, but it cannot trump Rule 60(c)(1)’s categorical text that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” with no carveout for (b)(4). Chief Justice Roberts’s minimalist approach is persuasive: applying (c)(1) to (b)(4) does not dilute due process because “reasonable time” can account for when the defect was discovered and whether reliance interests would be unfairly upset. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces the straightforward reading, and Espinosa (as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes) confirms (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights. Klapprott, as several colleagues note, only rejects importing the one-year cap from (b)(1)–(3); it does not erase (c)(1)’s separate reasonableness limit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest argument—that a judgment void for lack of personal jurisdiction is a nullity that may be attacked at any time—collides with the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which says any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be brought “within a reasonable time,” and (b)(4) is plainly within 60(b). Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett rightly stress we lack authority to create an atextual carveout where the Rule itself draws only one express timing distinction (the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3)). Justice Kagan’s invocation of Klapprott is important but, as she notes, it rejects importing the one-year limit into (b)(4) rather than erasing (c)(1)’s independent reasonableness requirement; Espinosa likewise cautions that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights. On a textualist and separation-of-powers approach, the proper course is to enforce (c)(1) as written and leave “reasonable time” to fact-bound application, not to announce a categorical “any time” rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument—that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack at any time—has force at common law, but it cannot override the Rules’ enacted text: Rule 60(c)(1) says any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and (b)(4) is plainly within that category. Chief Justice Roberts is right that a minimalist, rules-based holding applying (c)(1) to (b)(4) best serves finality and institutional legitimacy, especially in bankruptcy where reliance interests are acute. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Espinosa and Kemp strengthens the point that (b)(4) is not a “license to sleep on rights” and that “all” Rule 60(b) motions remain subject to the reasonable-time requirement. Klapprott, as multiple colleagues note, merely rejects importing the one-year cap into (b)(4); it does not erase (c)(1)’s separate reasonableness constraint.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s nullity maxim—that a void judgment may be attacked “at any time”—has force at common law, but it cannot override the Rules’ enacted text: Rule 60(c)(1) directs that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be brought “within a reasonable time,” and (b)(4) is unambiguously within 60(b). Justice Gorsuch’s point is decisive on a textualist reading: recognizing a categorical timeless exception would effectively write an atextual carveout into (c)(1), despite the Rule’s express decision to carve out only the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3). Justice Kagan’s discussion of Klapprott is also clarifying—Klapprott rejects importing the one-year limit into (b)(4), not the separate reasonable-time requirement—and Espinosa’s admonition that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights confirms that voidness and timeliness are distinct inquiries. Nothing raised in conference undermines that the proper disposition is to apply (c)(1) to (b)(4) and leave “reasonable time” to the lower courts’ fact-bound application.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention—that a void judgment is a nullity challengeable “at any time”—cannot override Rule 60(c)(1)’s express command that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be filed within a reasonable time, and Rule 60(b)(4) is plainly within that category. Justice Kagan’s reading of Klapprott is persuasive: it at most rejects importing the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3) into (b)(4), but it does not displace the freestanding reasonable-time requirement, which remains essential to procedural fairness and orderly administration. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on practical consequences in bankruptcy reinforces why reasonableness must be assessed case by case to prevent prejudice to third parties and destabilization of reliance interests, consistent with Espinosa’s warning that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights. Kemp’s observation—highlighted by Justice Barrett—that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to (c)(1) further confirms that the Rules’ timing discipline applies even when the underlying defect is serious, so long as courts remain attentive to due-process harms in evaluating what is “reasonable.”

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and that text naturally includes motions under Rule 60(b)(4) without carving out an atextual exception. Our cases counsel that voidness under Rule 60(b)(4) is narrowly confined to exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects, and the Court has recently reiterated that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement. Reading (c)(1) to apply also protects finality and reliance interests—especially acute in bankruptcy—while still permitting relief where a movant acts diligently upon learning of the defect. A minimalist resolution is to hold that (c)(1) governs (b)(4) motions, leaving to lower courts the case-specific inquiry into what is “reasonable” and any showing of prejudice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text governs: Rule 60(c)(1) provides that any motion “under Rule 60(b)”—which necessarily includes Rule 60(b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and courts are not free to carve out an atextual exception for void-judgment claims. While due process limits personal jurisdiction, Rule 60(b)(4) itself is the procedural vehicle Congress authorized for reopening final federal judgments, and it may be conditioned by the Rule’s express timing requirement consistent with finality interests. This Court in Espinosa emphasized that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” and Kemp likewise reiterated that “[a]ll” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement. Because petitioner disclaimed any alternative argument that its motion was filed within a reasonable time, the Sixth Circuit’s enforcement of Rule 60(c)(1) should be affirmed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is broad and mandatory: any motion “under Rule 60(b)”—which necessarily includes a motion under Rule 60(b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time.” Reading (b)(4) as categorically exempt would effectively add an atextual carve-out and would undermine finality and reliance interests, especially in settings like bankruptcy where long-delayed collateral attacks can disrupt administration and prejudice parties who could have cured service defects earlier. This Court’s statement in Kemp v. United States that “all” Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time reinforces that straightforward reading, while Espinosa’s narrow conception of “void” judgments and its emphasis on exceptional relief fit comfortably with enforcing reasonable-time limits. On these facts, where petitioner had actual notice years earlier and offered no justification for delay, the Sixth Circuit’s application of Rule 60(c)(1) is consistent with the Rules’ text and practical consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) says any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a “reasonable time,” and that plain text covers Rule 60(b)(4) as well; reading (b)(4) as timeless risks undermining finality in ways that fall hardest on third parties and vulnerable creditors who rely on judgments, particularly in bankruptcy administration. Espinosa reinforces that (b)(4) is not “a license for litigants to sleep on their rights” and construes “void” narrowly to exceptional cases, which fits a regime where courts can deny stale attacks when delay creates concrete prejudice and forfeits orderly process. Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement supports applying (c)(1) here, while still leaving meaningful protection because truly egregious due-process/personal-jurisdiction failures can be addressed when promptly raised. This approach preserves access to justice by allowing relief from genuinely void judgments but prevents strategic delay that can drain estates and impair remedies for those with the least power to absorb the disruption.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and that categorical language naturally includes Rule 60(b)(4) void-judgment motions. Espinosa supports that reading by emphasizing that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” reflecting a workable accommodation of due process with finality rather than an open-ended invitation to upset judgments years later. Nothing in Klapprott suggests otherwise; it merely recognizes that the one-year cap for Rule 60(b)(1)–(3) does not apply to (b)(4), leaving (c)(1)’s indefinite “reasonable time” constraint in place. In contexts like bankruptcy, enforcing a reasonableness limit coheres with the Rules’ structure and reliance interests while still allowing relief when the movant acts with appropriate diligence upon learning of the jurisdictional defect.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The rules’ text supplies the answer: Rule 60(c)(1) provides that any motion “under Rule 60(b)”—without carving out (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” so a court may deny even a void-judgment motion when the movant waits unreasonably long after learning of the defect. Reading (b)(4) to permit relief “at any time” would effectively add an atextual exception and would drain (c)(1)’s mandatory command of meaning, contrary to ordinary-textual understanding. Espinosa confirms that (b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional cases and does not transform the rule into a perpetual, costless option to upset settled judgments; finality and reliance interests, especially in bankruptcy administration, reinforce applying the rule as written. While due process forbids binding a party absent personal jurisdiction, Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement regulates the timing of the remedial motion, not the underlying constitutional rule, and it leaves room to grant relief promptly when the defect is timely raised.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Rules’ text is the starting point, and Rule 60(c)(1) says that a motion “under Rule 60(b)”—without carving out (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” which supports applying a reasonable-time constraint even to void-judgment claims. This Court’s recent statement in Kemp that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces that straightforward reading, and Espinosa likewise treats Rule 60(b)(4) as a narrow remedy while looking to treatise and circuit authority that does not license sleeping on rights. Finality and workability considerations are especially strong in bankruptcy administration, where delayed jurisdictional attacks can upset settled reliance and where earlier notice of a service defect could have allowed prompt cure. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and restraint, I would affirm the Sixth Circuit’s enforcement of Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement rather than creating a categorical no-deadline exception not found in the Rule’s text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: any motion "under Rule 60(b)"—which necessarily includes a motion under Rule 60(b)(4)—"must be made within a reasonable time," and we should not create an atextual carveout for void-judgment claims. That reading is reinforced by this Court’s statement in Kemp v. United States that "[a]ll" Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) is narrowly confined to exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects, but it does not displace Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing command; rather, the Rules’ structure accommodates both voidness and finality by requiring prompt invocation of the voidness claim. Applying the reasonable-time requirement here respects due process while recognizing reliance and finality interests—especially acute in bankruptcy—without converting jurisdiction into a waivable merits defense, because a timely Rule 60(b)(4) motion still requires the court to vacate a truly void judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and nothing in the text carves out Rule 60(b)(4) for special, limitless treatment—especially given that the Rule expressly creates distinct timing rules elsewhere (e.g., the one-year cap for 60(b)(1)–(3)). This Court’s decisions reinforce that voidness under 60(b)(4) is narrow and not a “license for litigants to sleep on their rights”: Espinosa held that a party with notice can forfeit service/notice objections through inaction, and Kemp recently reiterated that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement. A fact-sensitive reasonable-time standard best harmonizes due process with procedural fairness and practical consequences, including reliance and prejudice concerns that are acute in bankruptcy administration. Accordingly, I would affirm that 60(b)(4) relief is available only if sought within a reasonable time under 60(c)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party may move to set aside a default judgment as void for lack of personal jurisdiction under Rule 60(b)(4) at any time, or whether Rule 60(c)(1) requires that such a motion be filed within a "reasonable time."
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (relief from a judgment that "is void") and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) ("A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time"); with related due process/personal-jurisdiction principles as background.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio (a nullity), so a court has no discretion to let it stand based on delay; accordingly, Rule 60(c)(1)'s "reasonable time" requirement cannot cut off Rule 60(b)(4) relief, and the court's role is essentially to determine voidness and vacate if void regardless of the passage of time (including where service was defective).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the text of Rule 60(c)(1) applies to "any motion under Rule 60(b)," including Rule 60(b)(4), so even a voidness challenge must be brought within a reasonable time; this protects finality and reliance interests (particularly in bankruptcy, where reopening a long-administered estate can be highly disruptive) and allows consideration of prejudice and the movant's lack of justification for years-long delay.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (cited for the proposition that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010) (discussed regarding the scope of voidness and post-judgment attacks)
Klapprott v. United States, 335 U.S. 601 (1949) (discussed regarding timing and flexibility of Rule 60 relief and assumptions about no definite limit for void-judgment attacks)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962) (cited for inherent power to manage dockets)
World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013) (quoted for docket-management authority)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970) (cited re discretion/comity in referring enforcement/registration issues to the rendering court)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993) (cited regarding discretion/comity)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990) (cited in connection with the idea that void judgments may be attacked without time limits)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s nullity argument is the best case for petitioner, but under a minimalist, text-first approach it cannot justify reading an atextual categorical exemption into Rule 60(c)(1)’s unqualified command that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be brought within a reasonable time; a (b)(4) motion is still “under” 60(b). Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Kemp strengthens that conclusion by confirming this Court’s understanding that (c)(1)’s timing requirement applies across Rule 60(b) motions, making a carveout for (b)(4) especially hard to defend without rewriting the Rule. Espinosa also matters here: its warning that (b)(4) is not a “license to sleep on rights” supports a narrow holding that even assuming a serious jurisdictional defect, unreasonable, prejudicial delay—particularly where the movant had notice—can defeat relief, while leaving ample room for prompt challenges and for leniency where notice was lacking. That approach preserves due process without destabilizing final judgments and reliance interests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: Rule 60(c)(1) says a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and Kemp describes that timing rule as applying across Rule 60(b). But that reading treats “void” in Rule 60(b)(4) as if it meant merely “erroneous,” when the traditional and original understanding of a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is that it is a legal nullity—incapable of acquiring validity through delay. Espinosa’s admonition that (b)(4) is narrow addresses what counts as “void,” not whether a truly void judgment may be left in place because a court deems the challenge untimely; using (c)(1) to deny vacatur once voidness is established effectively gives operative legal effect to what the Rule labels void. Under a textualist lens attentive to terms of art, the best reconciliation is that “reasonable time” governs access to Rule 60(b) relief generally, but cannot be deployed to preserve a judgment that is void in the strict jurisdictional sense the Rule incorporates.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s “nullity” argument is the most serious objection, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) is enacted text stating without qualification that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and a (b)(4) motion is still “under” Rule 60(b). Espinosa matters here not merely for narrowing what counts as “void,” but also for its warning that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on one’s rights—language that is difficult to reconcile with a categorical, perpetual window. Kemp, as Justice Gorsuch notes, reinforces that (c)(1)’s timing regime applies across Rule 60(b), making an implied carveout for (b)(4) an atextual judicial rewrite. The proper reconciliation is to apply “reasonable time” with sensitivity to lack of notice (often making even a late filing reasonable) while still protecting finality and reliance against unjustified delay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s “nullity” argument squarely raises the worry that delay cannot "breathe life" into a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction, and I take seriously the due-process stakes for unserved or otherwise vulnerable parties. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) is enacted, unqualified text—“[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time”—and Kemp’s description of (c)(1) as applying across Rule 60(b) makes it especially hard to justify an implied categorical carveout for (b)(4) without rewriting the Rule. Espinosa matters here not just for narrowing what counts as “void,” but for rejecting (b)(4) as a license to sleep on rights; a flexible “reasonable time” standard can be applied empathetically to extend latitude where notice was lacking while still preventing strategic, prejudicial reopening of settled judgments (especially in bankruptcy). Under my pragmatic approach, that balance better protects access to justice for those truly deprived of notice while avoiding systemic harm to reliance interests from perpetual collateral attacks.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that a truly jurisdictionless judgment is a common-law “nullity” that cannot gain force through delay, but that premise does not answer the positive-law question the Rules pose: Rule 60(c)(1) says, without carveout, that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and (b)(4) is textually “under” 60(b). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (with Kemp), our recent cases have treated (c)(1)’s timing regime as applying across Rule 60(b), making it hard to justify an implied categorical exemption for (b)(4) without rewriting the Rule. Espinosa also matters: its admonition that (b)(4) is “narrow” and not a “license…to sleep on their rights” supports reading “void” narrowly and “reasonable time” as a real constraint, while still allowing courts to deem even long delays reasonable where notice was lacking or the party could not realistically appear. On my pragmatic textualist view, enforcing (c)(1) regulates access to the remedial mechanism rather than “validating” a void judgment, and it preserves workable finality/reliance protections—especially salient in bankruptcy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to stress the common-law intuition that a truly jurisdictionless judgment is a “nullity,” but our job begins with the enacted text: Rule 60(c)(1) states without exception that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and a (b)(4) request is still a motion “under Rule 60(b).” As the Chief Justice notes, Espinosa narrows what qualifies as “void” and cautions that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, which fits comfortably with applying (c)(1)’s reasonableness limit rather than creating an atextual perpetual carveout. Kemp’s broad description of Rule 60(c)’s timing regime applying across Rule 60(b) motions further undercuts rewriting the Rule to exempt (b)(4). The “nullity” concern can be handled within the textually prescribed standard by treating lack of notice or inability to appear as making even a late motion “reasonable,” while still protecting finality and reliance where delay is strategic or prejudicial.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that a truly void judgment was historically a nullity that cannot gain legal force through delay, but that common-law conception cannot override the Federal Rules’ enacted text governing access to post-judgment relief. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (with Kemp), Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and a (b)(4) motion is still “under” 60(b); creating a categorical exemption would be an atextual rewrite that is hard to justify institutionally. Espinosa matters because, as the Chief notes, it frames (b)(4) as a narrow safety valve and cautions it is not a “license” for litigants to sleep on rights, supporting a flexible reasonableness inquiry that can account for lack of notice while still protecting finality and reliance. Under my methodology, the best reconciliation is to apply (c)(1) to (b)(4) but construe “reasonable time” generously where due process failures prevented a timely challenge, rather than adopting an unlimited window as a matter of nullity theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s nullity argument is the strongest objection: at common law a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction was treated as void ab initio and not something that could be ‘cured’ by delay. But the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical—“[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time”—and a (b)(4) request is still a motion “under” Rule 60(b), so importing a perpetual, atextual carveout would override the Rule’s plain timing command. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Kemp reinforces that the Court has read (c)(1)’s timing regime to apply across Rule 60(b) motions, making it especially hard to justify an implied exception for (b)(4) by historical inference alone. Espinosa’s narrow conception of “void” further supports applying reasonableness: if (b)(4) is reserved for rare jurisdictional/due-process defects, the Rule can accommodate those cases through a flexible reasonable-time inquiry (particularly where notice was lacking) without destabilizing final judgments through unlimited collateral attacks.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s “nullity” conception is the strongest pushback, but it treats Rule 60(b)(4) as if it exists outside the Rules’ own remedial framework; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (with Kemp), Rule 60(c)(1) categorically governs the timing of “a motion under Rule 60(b),” and a (b)(4) filing is still such a motion. Applying a reasonable-time limit does not “validate” a jurisdictionally defective judgment so much as regulate when a federal court will deploy this collateral, equitable remedy—especially where the movant had notice and could have timely appeared. Espinosa matters here because it links the narrowness of (b)(4) to the idea that it is not a license to sleep on rights, which supports a flexible reasonableness inquiry that remains generous when notice was lacking but can deny strategic, prejudicial delay. On my pragmatic, fairness-focused view, that approach best balances due process for unserved parties with the real reliance and finality interests at stake in long-settled judgments.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and the most natural reading applies that limit to Rule 60(b)(4) as well, especially where the movant had notice and simply delayed. Espinosa underscores that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional cases and "does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights," recognizing forfeiture through inaction and the strong pull of finality. A reasonable-time requirement—flexible and fact-specific—preserves institutional legitimacy by protecting reliance interests and avoiding disruptive reopening of long-settled judgments (notably in bankruptcy), while still allowing vacatur when a genuinely void judgment is timely challenged. This narrow resolution hews to the Rules’ text and avoids creating an open-ended, no-time-limit collateral attack that would destabilize judgments and invite strategic delay.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(b)(4) authorizes relief when a judgment “is void,” and at the Founding and long after, a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction was treated as a nullity—incapable of acquiring legal force through delay. Reading Rule 60(c)(1)’s “reasonable time” requirement to validate an otherwise void judgment would invert that original meaning by allowing finality concerns to “breathe life” into a jurisdictional nullity, contrary to basic due process principles and the traditional understanding reflected in Rule 60(b)(4). Espinosa confirms that “void” is a narrow category tied to fundamental jurisdictional defects; once that showing is made, the court lacks discretion to enforce the judgment based on timeliness alone. To the extent any precedent suggests timeliness can bar a true voidness challenge, it should yield to the Rule’s text and the original public meaning of “void” as legal nonexistence.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Rules’ text is decisive: Rule 60(c)(1) states that “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in Rule 60(b)(4)’s “void” language creates an atextual, perpetual exception. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) is narrow and “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture through inaction and underscoring finality and reliance interests in judgments. Reading (c)(1) to constrain (b)(4) also serves practical consequences—especially in bankruptcy—by preventing years-late jurisdictional challenges that would disrupt settled distributions and impose substantial prejudice on innocent parties. The proper course is to apply the “reasonable time” standard flexibly, considering notice, diligence, and prejudice, rather than adopting a categorical no-time-limit rule untethered from the Rules’ text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and that text naturally encompasses Rule 60(b)(4) as well, allowing courts to consider delay and prejudice where reopening a long-settled judgment would inflict serious practical harms (as in bankruptcy administration). Espinosa construes Rule 60(b)(4) narrowly and reserves voidness relief for the “exceptional case” where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, which counsels against an unlimited, anytime attack that would undermine finality. Even where due process concerns are real, a “reasonable time” standard can accommodate them by treating lack of notice or inability to learn of the defect as strongly favoring timeliness, while still preventing strategic or unjustified years-long delay. This reading preserves access to justice for genuinely unserved parties yet protects vulnerable creditors and beneficiaries who rely on the stability of judgments in complex proceedings.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is broad—“[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time”—and it naturally includes motions brought under Rule 60(b)(4), so we should hesitate to carve out an atextual, categorical exception. Espinosa underscores that Rule 60(b)(4) is a “narrow” doctrine and “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture principles where a party with notice fails to raise service or jurisdiction objections in a timely way. Reading (b)(4) alongside (c)(1) yields a workable middle position: courts must vacate a truly void judgment when timely raised, but may deny relief where the movant unreasonably delays and reopening would impair finality and reliance, especially in contexts like bankruptcy administration. This approach preserves statutory coherence within Rule 60’s structure while still protecting due process by keeping the merits inquiry focused on whether the asserted jurisdictional defect actually renders the judgment void.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Rules’ text controls: Rule 60(c)(1) says “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and a Rule 60(b)(4) motion is, by its terms, “a motion under Rule 60(b).” Petitioner’s nullity theory cannot be squared with the Rules’ plain language, and this Court has recently reiterated in Kemp v. United States that Rule 60(c)’s “reasonable time” requirement applies to “all” Rule 60(b) motions. Espinosa confirms that (b)(4) is narrowly confined to truly jurisdictional or due-process defects and does not authorize open-ended collateral attacks whenever litigants delay; finality and reliance interests—especially acute in bankruptcy—are addressed by applying (c)(1) as written. If the balance is thought unwise, that is a policy question better handled through the Rules Enabling Act process, not by judicially carving (b)(4) out of (c)(1)’s categorical command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Rules’ text is the starting point: Rule 60(c)(1) says a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and that unqualified language naturally includes Rule 60(b)(4). Espinosa underscores that “void” in Rule 60(b)(4) is a narrow category and that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a general license for indefinite collateral attack, which supports applying (c)(1) to protect finality and reliance interests, especially in bankruptcy. Reading (b)(4) to override (c)(1) would effectively write the timing requirement out of the Rule for a major class of cases and invite serious practical disruption by reopening long-settled judgments. A “reasonable time” standard still respects due process by vacating truly void judgments when promptly raised, while allowing courts to account for unjustified, prejudicial delay in the exceptional posture of years-late challenges.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) provides that "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and the text contains no carveout for Rule 60(b)(4); as a textual matter, "a motion under Rule 60(b)" naturally encompasses (b)(4) motions. Espinosa’s narrow conception of voidness under Rule 60(b)(4)—reserving relief for exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects—supports reading (b)(4) as a limited, not boundless, mechanism within Rule 60’s overall structure rather than an implicit exemption from (c)(1). That reading also respects the Rules’ strong interest in finality while preserving meaningful relief where a movant acts with diligence, and it is methodologically consistent to apply the timing rule the drafters expressly imposed. Nothing in Kemp undermines this straightforward textual application; if anything, its emphasis on Rule 60’s time limits reinforces that Rule 60(c)(1) governs all Rule 60(b) motions absent an express exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states without carveout that "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and reading Rule 60(b)(4) as categorically exempt would override that text and undermine reliance interests and orderly administration—especially acute in bankruptcy where long-closed estates may be destabilized. Espinosa cabins Rule 60(b)(4) to exceptional cases and underscores finality by treating notice and the opportunity to be heard as central to whether a judgment is truly "void," not merely erroneous, which supports applying (c)(1)’s reasonableness inquiry to discourage sandbagging. This approach preserves procedural fairness by requiring prompt assertion of personal-jurisdiction defects so they can be cured (e.g., re-service) and by allowing courts to consider prejudice and practical consequences of years-long delay. Consistent with Kemp’s instruction that Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing rule governs Rule 60(b) motions generally, I would hold that even a (b)(4) motion must be filed within a reasonable time, while recognizing that what is “reasonable” may be generous where a party lacked notice or a meaningful chance to appear.
